content: Arthritis is a condition characterized by painful damage to the joints. It can occur as part of a systemic disorder or involve a single joint. The clinical presentation of arthritis typically includes joint pain (arthralgia), swelling, redness (erythema), warmth, and restricted movement. Arthritis can be classified based on the number of joints affected, the presence of inflammation, or the duration of symptoms. Osteoarthritis, also referred to as degenerative joint disease, is the most prevalent form of arthritis in the United States, affecting up to 10% of individuals over the age of 60. In contrast, inflammatory arthritis is commonly associated with systemic autoimmune diseases such as rheumatoid arthritis and systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE). In these systemic conditions, the disease course is usually chronic, and multiple joints (polyarticular involvement) are affected. On the other hand, infectious arthritis, such as septic arthritis, typically presents acutely and often involves a single joint (monoarticular involvement). Crystal-induced arthropathies, such as gout, result from the deposition of uric acid crystals in the joint space, leading to inflammation. While the clinical course and the presence of systemic manifestations are important for diagnosis, the definitive diagnostic method involves joint aspiration, fluid analysis, and microscopic evaluation. Imaging studies can also be useful in certain cases to assess the chronicity of the disease and detect structural changes in the joint and surrounding tissues. Prompt treatment is crucial, particularly for septic arthritis and inflammatory conditions, to prevent permanent joint damage and deformities. Primary Forms of Arthritis: Osteoarthritis Rheumatoid arthritis Septic arthritis Gout and pseudogout Juvenile idiopathic arthritis Still's disease Ankylosing spondylitis Differential Diagnosis of Monoarthritis: The differential diagnosis of monoarthritis depends on associated symptoms. For example: Monoarthritis with joint swelling Monoarthritis with fever Monoarthritis with weight loss Monoarthritis with claudication Monoarthritis with morning stiffness Monoarthritis with local erythema Monoarthritis with joint swelling and fever Monoarthritis with joint swelling, fever, and weight loss Differential Diagnosis of Polyarthritis: Similarly, the differential diagnosis of polyarthritis varies based on accompanying clinical features, such as: Polyarthritis with joint swelling Polyarthritis with fever Polyarthritis with weight loss Polyarthritis with claudication Polyarthritis with morning stiffness Polyarthritis with local erythema Polyarthritis with joint swelling and fever Polyarthritis with joint swelling, fever, and weight loss
